Joe Rogan thought it had to be a conspiracy theory: AI companies quietly buying millions of books, scanning them, and throwing the originals away. Then Jamie looked it up. ROGAN: "Oh my god, it's true." Anthropic had a code name for it: "Project Panama." The internal memo: "Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world." "We don't want it to be known that we are working on this." Rogan's reaction: "The training data is other people's work. It's books. That's what's insane." How it played out: Anthropic bought millions of books, cut off the spines, scanned every page and discarded them. Authors sued in Bartz v. Anthropic. The judge ruled the scanning of purchased books was fair use. The pirated books were another story. Anthropic had also downloaded millions from pirate sites, and that part cost it $1.5 billion, the largest copyright settlement in US history. About $3,000 per pirated book. Interested in AI? Impressive paper from CMU. Soon, we will have coding agents that can tune the entire stack, from prompts to token serving. This work experiments with coding agents to tune an LLM serving stack. They get Claude Sonnet 5.5 to build a serving system for Gemma E4B that delivers 4.87x the value per GPU dollar of the vLLM reference. ServerBench asks coding agents to design a complete, specialized serving system and decide how many concurrent sessions to run. The score is latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost, measured by replaying real coding sessions with their dependencies intact. An independent check verifies the system works. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, 22 of 33 runs produced a verified system and 13 beat the strongest baseline. The best designs raised capacity and chose the load to match it. Failed runs often shipped optimizations whose new code paths were never tested. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06841 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/serverbench-how-can-your-coding-agents-design-specialized-llm-serving-systems-2611.06841

Recommended benchmark from OpenAI on agents for everyday life tasks. They surveyed 3,837 US consumers to rank 148 life tasks by what people would pay an assistant to handle. Together, those tasks are worth over $1.7 trillion a year. LifeVal turns the most valuable of them into 169 agent tasks. Each one is written by someone who has done the task many times in real life, using their own ChatGPT conversations, memories, and files. The tasks include managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, and finding childcare. Every task comes with a rubric, a working environment and an offline copy of the web, and passes three rounds of human review. Scores rise steadily from GPT-5.2 to GPT-6 Astra. The most common failure for every model is a wrong answer or recommendation, often because the model missed a fact sitting in the user's past chats. On criteria tied only to past conversations, the win rate was 33%, compared with 48% for saved memories. If you build assistants with memory, test whether the agent actually finds what the user told it weeks ago. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06687 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/lifeval-evaluating-ai-model-performance-on-personalized-agentic-consumer-tasks-2611.06687

Own your intelligence stack, folks! We've reached the point where it's simply not possible to do reliable groundbreaking AI research (using autoresearch loops) with GPT or Claude. I constantly get hammered with inaccurate refusals. This is sad! They should at least spend time fixing their classifiers. But over the last year, I've learned to build my own thing and own more of the intelligence stack. My advice: never lock yourself into any of these vendors if you really care about your business and customers. Imagine trying to stay at the frontier and depending on these models. You simply won't be able to. They'll refuse requests (at the model and harness layer), and that will hurt you profoundly. If you run a small research lab, or even plan to do minimal research (we all should be trying to) in the future (with RSI pipelines) for your business, you need to get this part right. Many companies have already realized this and have started building their own intelligence stack. From the harness to training and serving their own models. It's not easy, but it is the way. It's very clear to me that open-source models are truly the only path forward.
As is Gary, Indiana. San Francisco is pretty from above 🥰

By the way, the research that I am talking about is simple research loops (tuning harnesses) for hill climbing. It doesn't even try to train a model or anything. I don't think people realize the implications of this yet. If you plan to participate in a world of RSI, you'll struggle to use these models for anything useful. And this doesn't only apply to research labs; it applies to any business using AI in its products.

What I'm seeing across the industry right now is that the biggest bottleneck to AI adoption isn't model capabilities. It's data infrastructure. Today, we're expanding the Eon Data Foundation with the launch of Eon Yukon, a new serverless data engine purposely built to change that. AI agents need fresh, contextualized data to act. Specialized models need a continuous feed of data and feedback to improve. Both are still served by a stack, an architecture, and methods built for dashboards: -Spark and Flink clusters sized for peak, plus compaction jobs to keep tables usable. -A pipeline and a copy for every consumer, staged bronze to silver to gold. -Hand-written jobs, wired together by an orchestrator and kept alive by specialists. The result: shipping data is complicated, risky, and expensive. While coding agents ship apps in hours, they rarely build or run data pipelines. The data is too volatile, and a mistake costs too much. With Yukon, data moves from ingestion to processing to serving in one continuous flow, without the infrastructure and pipelines traditionally required to connect them. Events become compacted, sorted, deduplicated Iceberg tables within seconds. Real-time aggregations run inline, with fully managed state. Agents and applications can access fresh data with sub-millisecond latency through a Redis-compatible API or through our SQL and spark compatible query engine. Beyond moving and serving data, Yukon makes it continuously understandable - Live column-level statistics, accessible through MCP, give agents visibility into the data. Built-in monitoring, sampling, and data minimization help teams maintain control. At 1M events/sec and equal freshness, Yukon used 4x less compute than Spark and 7x less than Flink. The benchmark is public: run it yourself with Eon’s ingest-bench. This is another major step toward our vision of an Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era, built to both protect enterprise data and unlock its full potential. Media

Your company's SOPs, support tickets, and internal docs could be worth six figures. If your business has 30+ full-time employees, you may already have something valuable to AI companies. Think about all the situations your team has documented over the years: - How to train new hires - When to approve an exception - How to resolve complicated customer issues - What to do when a process breaks Those answers are sitting in SOPs, CRM records, support tickets, project histories, and internal knowledge bases. What's valuable is the decision-making behind them. These records show how people handle real situations, including the ones that don't follow the usual playbook. And that's useful for training AI agents to handle actual business tasks. That's the idea behind @micro1_ai's Company Data Partnerships program. micro1 pays qualifying businesses to license operational data they already have. For approved partnerships, payments start at $100K+ and can go higher depending on the amount, quality, and uniqueness of the data. Companies keep ownership of their underlying data. And micro1 says personal and identifying information is removed or transformed before the data is shared with third parties. They're looking across industries for established businesses with substantial English-language documentation. If that sounds like your company, it's worth seeing if you qualify: https://company.micro1.ai/register/?referralCode=72108c0b-3efa-456b-8b70-4a75fcc3565b&utm_source=referral&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=job_referral

The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds for Physical AI. Most embodied prediction tasks like object localization, robot trajectory planning, and dense 3D motion are fixed-length float vectors. For example, a bounding box is always 6 tokens, a 10-waypoint robot arm trajectory is 54: we know these beforehand. Instead of decoding one token at a time, we can output the entire geometric shape in one go. VFlash enables up to 12x faster action decoding and a 5.1x overall robot inference speedup on edge GPUs like the Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. What’s surprising is that it ends up even more accurate than the VLM backbone, with up to 61% lower 3D trajectory error. The intuition is that VFlash avoids the cascading errors of autoregressive decoding, where every coordinate is written in ink and every later point loses the chance to backspace. Everything that moves will be autonomous, and everything autonomous will need to think on its own chip. The next inference revolution is physical reasoning at the speed of reflex. And as always, it’s open paper, open source! Link in thread: Media

“没必要招一个比你更弱的人。大部分团队 2–3 人就够了。”这是今天 AI Engineer 大会上，一位 OnlyFans 顾问跟我说的。他早期是滴滴的 AI 负责人，后来去了美国 Roblox，他非常不建议现在创业团队招人。 我们聊到社交，他说美国做 AI 线上社交已经很卷了，现在美国反而在转做线下社交，见面、互动、一起吃饭这些。在他们看来，Telegram 不是一个好的社交渠道。而且不建议我去旧金山，因为甲方和客户都不在那。 谈到现在AI创业的人，他说现在只能做非常垂直的赛道 整个展区摊位，有一些做量化的（Optiver）、做培训的、做 Agent 评估（Evaluation）的，还有 http://You.com 这类给 Agent 用的搜索工具。 前 Cursor 的 Ryo Lu，@ryolu_ 从旧金山搬回台北了，他觉得旧金山到处都是KPI，什么都要被优化，受不了那种硅谷的氛围。 他今天的演讲题目是：当我们什么都能做的时候，我们要做什么？ 其实是现在大家经常讨论的话题，当工具越来越强，开始替你做所有判断，甚至直接给你一个很好、很完整的结果。比如，你让它做一个日记 App，它会帮你设好提醒、心情指数。这当然没什么不对，但这真的是你想要的吗？很可能只是AI大量参考了其他人的结果。 而你在被动接受一个完整的结果，但你并没有参与其中。 他自己从旧金山搬到台北，也是在实践这件事。要保留人 做不同选择的自由。 包括我再次见到的这个朋友在内，很多人都讲到，Agent 性价比更高、算力更强、更强的英伟达…，但到头来还是要去解决服务人的需求、要人和人去见面。还有人聊到了宠物医疗。 大家都在说 Agent 经济、Agent 卖东西，但现场真正反复出现的问题是：Agent 怎么服务于人的需求。 人 要参与到 AI 生成的过程里，从 Prefill 到 Decode

Grok Build packed a serious upgrade into this release, making multi-agent workflows more reliable, easier to control, and much smoother to manage Background agents and workflows now stay visible as active work on the dashboard, workflow status shows how many agents are still running, and stop controls work even when approval prompts are open. Permission rules that fail to load now trigger warnings instead of silently being ignored Session recovery is also more reliable, manually saved file edits are better protected, and Ctrl+L can now quote selected messages directly into your prompt. There’s also improved keyboard navigation, better terminal compatibility, and fixes across skills, hooks, file handling, and session management Another strong push toward making Grok Build a dependable environment for running entire teams of AI agents Release Notes: v1.0.75 Features: • Permission rules that don't load, such as a rule that doesn't parse or a .claude/settings.json that isn't valid JSON, show a warning when a session opens instead of being skipped silently. • Cmd+Up / Cmd+Down and Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End move the cursor to the start or end of the whole prompt, and with Shift they select to there. • Send now shows as Enter Enter in the footer where Ctrl+Enter arrives as plain Enter, such as inside tmux with its default settings. • Esc on a /btw side question that hasn't been answered yet cancels it, instead of letting it run on and reopening the panel when the answer arrives. • Clicking a link or file that can't open, such as over SSH with no display, shows why, for example "Can't open links over SSH". • Left on an empty prompt opens the dashboard from any session or the welcome screen, not only from a session you opened from the dashboard. • The /btw question in the panel's title can be selected with the mouse and is copied to the clipboard when you release, like the answer text. • Workflow status lines say how many agents are still running instead of how many exist. • Ctrl+L in the scrollback adds the selected message or highlighted text to the prompt as a quote. Open Extensions with /plugins. Bug Fixes: • Notes above a queued prompt, such as a model switch result or a ready worktree, stay on screen when the prompt starts instead of scrolling out of view. • Stop buttons in the dock stop a background run while its approval card is open, instead of doing nothing until you answer the card. • Rejecting a change keeps edits you saved to the file yourself, even when Grok missed the save, instead of overwriting them. • grok --resume <id> opens the session in the folder it was recorded in, wherever you launch Grok from, instead of refusing. • Windows: on older consoles such as plain cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell windows, the ▶, ⏸ and ◌ marks in todo, workflow and list rows show as characters the console can draw instead of empty boxes. • Generated image and video paths with wide characters such as Chinese, Japanese or emoji fit their row and keep the file name, and Windows paths keep it too. • The rewind confirmation no longer crashes Grok on a short terminal or when you shrink the window while it's open. • Footer and status bars in narrow terminals drop or shorten the items that don't fit, instead of painting them over each other or cutting buttons off. • Cut-off Fetch, Web Search and MCP tool output ends with the same … +N lines · <key> to view all row as code cells, naming your viewer key, and one hidden line reads +1 line. • 16-color terminals show the paste label and tool accents in the muted gray other secondary text uses, and the paste label's brackets no longer vanish on the light theme. • A question card's Enter:submit button, the dashboard session popup's [✗] and collapsed workflow rows highlight under the mouse pointer like other clickable controls. • Emoji and keycap symbols such as ⚠️ or #️⃣ are measured at the width the terminal draws them, so rows no longer run past their box or lose their …. • /export to a named pipe that nothing is reading fails right away instead of freezing Grok until it is killed. • Typing a digit or symbol while the scrollback has focus, with vim keys off, moves focus to the prompt and types it there, as letters already do. ? still opens the command palette. • grok sessions delete no longer fails with "Directory not empty" when another process is still writing into the session's folder. • Dashboard rows stay in Working while a session's background subagents or workflow runs are going, and stopping the row ends them. • Code blocks inside quotes render every line under the quote's bars, quote copies turn reference links into inline links, and lines after multi-line math are numbered correctly. • Disabling a project's hook in /hooks applies only to that repository, instead of also skipping hooks with the same name in other repositories. • Turning a skill on or off in the Skills tab saves only [skills].disabled to config.toml, so an organization's managed skill folders and ignore list keep applying. • /btw starts a side question only when it begins the message. A /btw later in the text goes to the main conversation as typed. Today’s GPT-6 Cyber release is a meaningful step for defenders: stronger vulnerability research and better alignment. We’ve already been using GPT-6 Cyber alongside GPT-6 Astra with Daybreak to harden our own systems, finding weaknesses, validating their impact, and developing fixes. Even after years @OpenAI, model capabilities continue to surprise me. One small example came from testing a prerelease version of GPT-6 Astra earlier this summer. We were examining tools used across our research infrastructure and one of our research infra leads, Michael Dalton, was looking into some low risk areas like a math task grader that used SymPy, a mathematics library, to check answers. In an offline test, the submitted answer used characters that looked like ordinary letters to get past the grader’s checks. It caused the grader to run a shell command that printed “4242”, while still returning the expected result, 1/2. The grader marked the answer correct. A valid math answer had become a way to run code inside the grader - diagram below. This is the kind of vulnerability that can be very hard for a human to find, even with a fuzzer. It takes connecting how input validation and evaluation interact, constructing an input that passes the checks but triggers unintended behavior, and recognizing the failure even when the final answer is correct. Models can reason across those pieces and help uncover classes of vulnerabilities that are difficult to spot when reviewing components in isolation. That’s why it’s important for more defenders to use models with Daybreak to find and fix vulnerabilities in their own systems. Whether it’s a potentially internet-melting bug like PHP2Shell or a subtle but important issue like this grader bug, finding it before an attacker does gives defenders time to act. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers - let us know if you’re interested: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdQu8mNYXDpUW_0kRS6JBWBPMWfUjjxi6xLi8AkFPObLupkpg/viewform Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber: a major advance in security research that pairs stronger capabilities with better model alignment. 18 of the 20 best open models today are Mixture-of-Experts. Dense is basically over. And yet the know-how to train a good MoE still lives mostly in the heads of a handful of teams. So we spent 800k GPU hours running the experiments ourselves and wrote everything down. Super happy to finally release "The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook", free and open, organized around the questions training teams hit: - how many experts, how big, shared or not? - why is half my step spent in all-to-all, and how do I hide it? - why is my run 25x slower with no error in the logs? - softmax, sigmoid or sqrt(softplus) router, and why keep it in fp32? - aux loss or DeepSeek's loss-free bias? - upcycle a dense checkpoint or train from scratch? - can I serve with fewer experts per token than I trained with? ⚠️ Warning: it's long (~70k words, budget a few days, sorry) but with 55 interactive figures, code you can run and numbers from our own runs. Read it here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/moe-blogpost Media

Banger paper on RSI with foundation model systems. (bookmark it) Seriously, I highly recommend this paper if you want to start experimenting with RSI in your own company. Lots of great insights and tips. They propose Recursa, which raises DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from 30.0% to 55.0% all-pass on held-out legal tasks, without a stronger teacher or human experts. The model weights stay the same. The gain comes from a knowledge repository the system writes for itself. The repository stores domain skills, instructions on when to use them, memories of past tasks, and reflections. Recursa first builds it from domain materials. Then parallel learners run tasks and propose fixes, and only validated fixes get merged back. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Qwen3.8-Flash goes from 35.0% to 46.0% with the same loop. If you are adapting an agent to a new domain, try a validated skill repository before reaching for fine-tuning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04035 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/recursa-toward-recursively-self-improving-foundation-model-systems-2611.04035
